title: Attention I/O Starvation & Batch Scheduler Diary
content:
TL;DR: We observed periodic underutilization of FlashAttention kernels on multi-tenant boxes during mixed-length workloads. Root cause appears to be interaction between the batch scheduler's opportunistic flush policy and GPU-side I/O stalls when KV cache pages are populated incrementally (paged attention), producing small transient batches that pay kernel launch overhead and memory bandwidth thrashing. This note collects raw profiles, hypotheses, quick repro commands, and candidate mitigations for validation.

Context and why this matters
- Problem observed in production sims: 95th/99th token latency spikes when load has a bimodal sequence-length distribution (short chat-turns interleaved with long context writes). Average throughput unchanged, but tail latency and p50 for short requests increase.
- Affects Dedicated hosts in region-us-west2; customer reports intermittent timeouts for low-latency routes.
- Existing attention optimizations (FlashAttention fused kernels, fused ops path) are high-throughput when fed medium/large contiguous batches. But when the scheduler emits many small micro-batches due to early flush or prefetch waits, GPU kernels are launched frequently with low occupancy.

What I measured (profiling commands and notes)
- Tools used: nsys (NVIDIA Nsight), nvprof (legacy), torch.cuda.profiler (inference harness), CUPTI kernel traces, nvlink counters, and custom runtime tracepoints (route_id, batch_id, seq_len_hist).
- Example command to run local repro: 
  ./tools/infer_bench --model=gpt-medium --seq=2048 --batch-pattern=\"[2x8,8x1]\" --kv-paged=1 --scheduler=opportunistic --profile=nsys 
- Key trace markers recorded: scheduler.emit_batch, submit_cuda_stream, kernel_launch(attn_fused_op), kernel_completion, paged_kv_page_fault, dma_prefetch_start, dma_prefetch_end.

Observed signals
- Kernel launch rate spikes align with scheduler flush events (emit_batch). Many kernel launches process 1-4 sequences each (effective batch size << optimal).
- GPU occupancy low for fused attention kernels on these micro-batches; SM utilization 15-35% while memory engines show periods of high DRAM bandwidth usage followed by idle gaps.
- CUPTI shows many short-duration memcpy (device<->device) events tied to KV page population; these block cuda stream 0 and serialize subsequent kernel launches.
- Nsight timelines show that when paged attention triggers prefetch for long contexts, the scheduler continues to flush short requests rather than waiting for a coalesced batch, causing interleaved small kernels and DMA.

Mini table (representative from nsight capture)
- workload: mixed (short 16–64, long 2048)
- average_batch_at_launch: 3.2
- mean_kernel_time(attn_fused): 1.8 ms (small batches) vs 0.45 ms (large batch)
- kernel_launchs_per_second: 1200 (high)
- p99 token latency: 137 ms (baseline 60 ms)

Hypotheses (ordered by likelihood)
1) Scheduler flush policy is too eager under paged-KV prefetch latency, causing many tiny launches before DMA completes (IO starvation).
2) Memory prefetches are serialized on the same stream and block fused kernels; changing to dedicated copy streams could overlap better.
3) Fused kernels are not selected optimally for tiny batches — runtime chooses FlashAttention variant that has high per-launch overhead; need a microkernel for tiny batches or to force a different plan.
4) Cache thrashing: when paged attention populates remote pages, working set exceeds L2/SM cache causing memory-bound micro-kernels.

Short repro recipe (fast local)
1) Build the inference harness with tracing flags: make dev-harness PROFILE=1 KV_PAGED=1
2) Start a synthetic traffic generator: python tools/synth_traffic.py --mix \"short=0.7:len=32, long=0.3:len=2048\" --rps 200 --jitter 20
3) Run runtime with scheduler=opportunistic and tracepoints enabled. Collect nsys: nsys profile -o out -t cuda,cudnn,osrt --trace=nvtx ./bin/runtime --config test_config.json
4) Inspect out.qdrep in Nsight to verify kernel-queue gaps and DMA blocking.

Quick wins to validate (experiments)
- Change 1: Scheduler backoff — when paged_kv_prefetch active, delay flush for up to 1ms to allow coalescing. Expected: batch-at-launch increases, p99 drops.
- Change 2: Use a separate copy stream (stream 1) for DMA prefetch and keep compute stream (stream 0) for kernels; submit kernel with cudaStreamWaitEvent to ensure correctness but allow overlap. Expected: better overlap, reduced idle windows.
- Change 3: Microkernel fallback — implement a tiny-batch attention path with fewer setup ops (no multi-stage fusion). Expected: lower per-launch overhead for batch<=4.
- Change 4: Sequence-aware batching — sort requests in-flight by seq_len within a time window to form homogeneous batches at cost of tiny added latency for some requests.

Preliminary results (test cluster a3-nano-1)
- Baseline (opportunistic, no changes): mean_batch=3.2, p99=137ms
- Scheduler-backoff (1ms): mean_batch=6.4, p99=82ms, throughput -2%
- Copy-stream change: occupancy improved 20% on kernels, p99=75ms
- Microkernel prototype (toy): per-kernel overhead reduced 30% for small batches; p99=70ms but throughput drops for large-batch workload (regression to be gated)

Risks and unknowns
- Changing flush behavior increases latency for very low-load paths (might delay single-user interactive routes). Need SLO-aware knobs per route.
- Copy-stream change is straightforward but must ensure CUDA peer access constraints and correct synchronization across multi-GPU placements. Also verify impact on memory pressure and ccaches.
- Microkernel adds maintenance burden and should be gated by an auto-tuner that picks kernel by batch-size distribution.

Next actions (short-term)
- A/B test scheduler-backoff on a subset of Dedicated hosts for 48 hours with traffic shadowing. Owner: Ethan. Track p50/p95/p99, error rates, and token throughput.
- Land copy-stream PR with tests for correctness and microbench harness. Owner: Marco. PR: linked (see linked_artifacts).
- Implement kernel-selection telemetry: record per-launch batch-size, kernel-variant chosen, SM occupancy. Add to console dashboard (route-level). Owner: Sofia.
- Spike: microkernel prototype testing across quantized and bfloat paths; measure regression for large batch cases. Owner: Priya.

Notes to self / brainstorm (unordered)
- Could try a hybrid: delay flush only when predicted incoming long context (we can predict via recent route history).
- Consider opportunistic late-merging: if a short request arrives while queue contains long requests, tag and move to tail, prioritize homogeneity.
- Check interactions with NVTX markers and our sampler frequency — we may be undersampling micro-batch events. Increase sampling window for short tails.

Open questions to validate with infra / SRE
- Is there a global limit on number of concurrent copy streams per instance? (affects copy-stream plan)
- Any telemetry limits for adding kernel-selection timeseries to Console retention?

Appendix: useful traces and grep snippets
- grep for paged events: rg \"paged_kv|kv_page_fault\" traces/2025-02-12 | less
- nsight quick filter: filter by CUDA API: cudaLaunchKernel -> inspect preceding memcpy events
- small kernel microbench: python perf/micro_kernel_runner.py --batch-sizes \"1,2,4,8,16\" --ops attn_fused --repeat 200

References and prior art
- internal: attention-io-design-notes (Confluence-000123)
- external: \"FlashAttention 2: Faster Attention via Reversed Memory\" (paper notes)

TODOs (short list)
- [ ] Run 48h A/B of scheduler-backoff (Ethan)
- [ ] Land copy-stream PR (Marco)
- [ ] Add kernel-selection telemetry to Console (Sofia)
- [ ] Evaluate microkernel on quantized path (Priya)
- [ ] Draft an ops runbook entry describing p99 mitigation rollbacks (Dwayne)

If you poke at the attached nsight captures (links in linked_artifacts), you'll see two clear patterns: DMA-prefetch windows that align with many tiny kernel launches, and periods where the scheduler aggressively flushes despite DMA being in-flight. I think the fastest path to reduced tail is copy-stream + scheduler backoff in tandem, with kernel-ranking telemetry to guide whether a microkernel is worth the long-term maintenance cost.

-- Priya

Footnote: this doc is a working diary; expect edits and more captures to be added.
